body.text: Traditional owners reconnect with country to help guide national park future
In short:
About 15 traditional owners have returned to country in western NSW to discuss the future of a former station set to become a national park.
The station was privately owned for 150 years.
What's next?
The Avenel Mount Westwood Estate will be gazetted as a national park.
It was an emotional moment for Mike Gilby when his feet sunk into the dirt of his ancestral country for the first time.
For the previous 150 years, the land had been a privately owned station, but now the vast property is among those bought by the New South Wales government to turn into national park.
It means traditional owners such as Mr Gilby, a Malyangapa, Barkandji and Wangkumara man, have been able to set foot on it for the first time.
Growing up in north-west NSW, the lands of his people were his childhood playground, but the private property was off limits.
"That wasn't as a result of we didn't want to visit. It was a pastoral lease, it was private property and respecting that, you let the pastoralists run it as a business," he said.
"As an adult, coming back here in my late 50s, all those memories are still there, and they're just embedded as part of me."
Mr Gilby was one of more than a dozen traditional owners who recently gathered at the former station, some of them visiting for the first time.
The group was tasked with helping to plan the future of the new national park.

"It just brings back memories as a young black kid growing up out here with all our families, and it wasn't just Aboriginal families, it was everyone. We were a part of the community and we still are today," he said.
Community at forefront of park decisions
The Avenel Mount Westwood reserve encompasses four former pastoral stations with a combined area of 121,000 hectares.
The stations were purchased by the NSW government in 2021 and the park is set to be one of the largest in the state.

The reserve is on the lands of the Malyangapa and Wilyakali people, and representatives from each group make up the Avenel Mt Westwood Aboriginal Co-management Committee, which helps to guide decisions on how the park will be managed.
Mr Gilby said community engagement was at the forefront of their decision-making.
"It's a pastoral area that we operate within, and we need to be considerate of our neighbours who are still operating pastoral properties next door to us," he said.

"But it's also about reconnecting our family, our young people, and putting people back in the landscape, I suppose, under the guise of now working alongside [the National Parks and Wildlife Service].
"It's setting in place the parameters that the next generations can pick up and take forward. Everything we do at the table today, the beneficiaries are our young people in all of this."

The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) estate features a diverse range of ecosystems, including sand plains and sandhills, stony desert, shrubland, rocky hills and flood plain watercourses.
It is also home to 38 different species of threatened flora and fauna.

Aboriginal artefacts have been found across the property, including grinding plates and stones, digging sticks and more, which Mr Gilby said would be preserved and managed with guidance from the committee.
"Now, under [the ownership of NPWS], we're able to look at the landscape through a conservation lens and a cultural lens," he said.
Red sand and big dreams
Looking after the reserve is experienced station manager Makhalia Girdler, who will also live there.
The senior field officer has spent the past 12 years managing the property next door with her husband.
"Running a national park is very similar to managing property, sheep and cattle. There's not much difference in it," she said.
"We're still conserving land, watching the grasses, making sure there's minimal impact."
Managing the reserve means spending most days weeding, maintaining and building station infrastructure and controlling invasive species.
"We're trying to keep the [pig] numbers down. I've been successful with that at the moment; I'm getting hundreds in one night," Ms Girdler said.
The manager, who grew up on a station just down the road, said she could not imagine living anywhere else.
"It's still the isolation, the red sand, that's in my blood. It's my community, my local neighbours. I've known them all my life."
As for the future of the reserve, she has ambitious plans.
"I'd like it to be an education area where we can get the university students back out and study geology or eco-science," she said.
For Mr Gilby, he is excited at the reserve's potential for educating younger generations.
"We want to take the opportunity to actually immerse our next generations back into these landscapes," he said.
"It's about how we leverage off those opportunities to create, be it employment, culture camps, education.
"So it's not just maintaining the biodiversity in the landscape but also [asking], how do we put people back into the landscape to be a part of the bigger picture?"
